items.prompt: What is the difference between "technical risk" and "business risk" as this unit defines them?
choices: Technical risk is a fact about system behavior described in engineering terms; business risk is the same fact re-expressed as what it could cost the business
Technical risk only ever applies to security issues, while business risk only ever applies to scaling and growth issues
They're really the same thing underneath — just one version described at greater length than the other
Technical risk is always, by definition, more severe in practice than any equivalent business risk
items.explanation: Technical risk and business risk describe the same underlying fact from two different vantage points — the mechanism versus what it costs the business — not two different kinds of problems.
items.reference:
Technical risk

62% pool utilization

Business risk

$18K/min lost, by week 27

Why: same fact, two vantage points — one for the engineer, one for the decision-maker.
items.learnMore:
One fact, two framings

Marcus's checkout database was really running at 62% connection-pool utilization — that's a true, precise technical fact. It's also true that, at current growth, the same fact means checkout starts failing under normal load around week 27, and is already breached at Black-Friday-level traffic today. Neither framing is more accurate than the other; they answer different questions. "62%" answers "what is the system doing." "$18K/minute, by week 27" answers "what should I do about it." Translating technical risk to business risk means deliberately re-expressing the first framing into the second — not replacing the technical analysis, just re-stating its conclusion in units the decision-maker already uses.

items.prompt: Why does a non-technical leader need the business-risk framing rather than the technical framing, even if the technical facts are explained clearly?
choices: Because the business-risk framing is expressed in units (cost, dates, customers) the leader already uses to compare this ask against every other decision they're weighing
Because technical framing of a risk is always, strictly speaking, factually wrong or incomplete
Because business leaders are generally incapable of understanding any technical vocabulary at all
Because business framing is simply shorter overall and takes noticeably less time to say out loud
items.explanation: A leader routinely weighs many competing asks (hiring, budget, other proposals) that all arrive denominated in cost and timeline — a risk stated only in technical terms simply isn't in a comparable unit, regardless of how clearly it's explained.

items.prompt: As this unit defines it, what is "probability" in a translated risk explanation?
choices: How likely the bad outcome is, and importantly, how that likelihood is changing over time if nothing is done
A single, flat yes/no statement about whether the bad outcome will eventually happen
The raw number of engineers on the team who personally agree the risk is real
A percentage figure that by definition never needs any timeframe attached to it
items.explanation: Probability in this framework isn't a static label — it's explicitly tied to a trend over time, which is what makes a concrete "by when" possible.
items.reference:
📈 Probability — likelihood, plus how it's changing over time
🗓️ Not static — tied to a trend, not a one-time label

Why: a probability that changes over time is what makes a concrete deadline possible in the first place.
items.learnMore:
Probability as a trend, not a snapshot

It would be easy to state probability as a single frozen number — "there's a 70% chance of an incident." The unit's framing is more useful because it treats probability as something moving along a trend: checkout utilization at 62% today isn't itself the risk; it's the trajectory (8% monthly growth) that turns 62% into 100% around week 27 if nothing changes. That trajectory is what lets Marcus give Elena an actual date instead of a static severity label, and it's also what makes the "if nothing changes" framing honest — it's explicit that the projection assumes no intervention, which is exactly the choice being put in front of the decision-maker.

items.prompt: As this unit defines it, what is "impact" in a translated risk explanation?
choices: The concrete cost if the risk materializes, ideally expressed in units the listener already tracks — dollars, customers, hours of downtime
A technical severity rating of some kind, like "critical" or "high", assigned by engineering
The raw number of lines of code in the codebase that are affected by the underlying issue
How embarrassing the issue would be for the team to have to explain publicly to customers
items.explanation: Impact means naming the actual cost in the listener's own units, not restating the technical severity a different way.
items.reference:
💵 Impact — a concrete cost, not a severity word
📊 Listener's units — dollars, customers, downtime hours

Why: a severity label like "critical" doesn't tell a business leader what happens — a dollar figure does.
items.learnMore:
Impact in the listener's units

"Critical severity" is a technical classification useful for triaging tickets among engineers — it doesn't tell a COO what actually happens if the risk materializes. The unit's rewrite instead names roughly $18,000 in lost sales per minute of checkout downtime during peak hours, plus the reputational cost of a visible failure during a high-traffic sale event. Those are units Elena already uses to weigh this ask against a marketing budget or a hiring plan. The translation work is specifically converting a severity classification into a cost the listener can put on the same scale as everything else competing for their attention.

items.prompt: What is an "exposure window" (the "by when"), as this unit defines it?
choices: The specific date, milestone, or event by which the risk stops being hypothetical and becomes real if nothing changes
The raw number of hours a given system has been running continuously without a restart
A fancier synonym for the word "urgent" used mainly to sound more precise in a meeting
The amount of time it takes an engineer to actually write and ship the corresponding fix
items.explanation: The exposure window is a specific, checkable point in time — not a vague sense of urgency dressed up as a technical term.
items.reference:
🗓️ Exposure window — a specific date or event, not a feeling
✅ Checkable — the listener can verify it against their own calendar

Why: "soon" can't be checked against a calendar; "week 27" or "Black Friday" can.
items.learnMore:
Why a date beats a feeling

"This is getting urgent" is a judgment call the listener has no way to independently verify — they either trust the engineer's sense of urgency or they don't. "Around week 27" or "already breached at Black-Friday-level traffic" is a claim the listener can check against their own calendar: is week 27 before or after a product launch, a budget cycle, the actual Black Friday date? A specific exposure window converts a subjective urgency claim into an objective planning input, which is exactly what lets Elena decide whether this competes with, or can wait behind, everything else on her plate.

items.prompt: What does this unit mean by "catastrophizing" a technical risk?
choices: Describing the risk as more certain or more severe than the evidence actually supports
Explaining a given risk to a business leader using far too much technical jargon and detail
Flatly refusing to give a business leader any kind of timeline at all for the risk
Asking for considerably more budget than the proposed fix would actually require to ship
items.explanation: Catastrophizing means overstating certainty or severity beyond what the evidence shows — not simply being thorough or specific.
items.reference:
🔺 Catastrophizing — overstates certainty/severity
🔻 Minimizing — understates certainty/severity

Why: both directions cost credibility for future warnings — the fix is calibration, not picking a side.
items.learnMore:
Two ways to lose credibility

Marcus could have said "this could take down the whole platform any day now" — more dramatic than the evidence supports, since the actual projection is a gradual capacity ceiling around week 27, not an imminent platform-wide failure. That's catastrophizing. He could equally have said "it's probably fine, we'll deal with it eventually" — which understates a risk that's already breached at Black-Friday-level traffic today. That's minimizing. Both distort the same underlying evidence in opposite directions, and both teach the listener to discount future warnings once the gap between the claim and what actually happened becomes visible. The calibrated version states the trend and the date as they actually are.

Focusing the explanation purely on the financial impact while ignoring everything else entirely
items.explanation: Minimizing means understating certainty or severity relative to the evidence — often to avoid an uncomfortable conversation, leaving the listener under-informed.
items.reference:

🔻 Minimizing — understates certainty/severity

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, why did Elena respond "keep an eye on it" instead of approving or rejecting a specific action?
choices: Marcus's explanation never gave her a cost, a date, or a decision to actually make — so there was nothing concrete to approve or reject
Elena simply didn't believe the technical facts that Marcus had presented to her
Elena was genuinely too busy that day to give the issue any real consideration at all
The checkout database problem Marcus described wasn't actually a real, existing problem
items.explanation: "Keep an eye on it" is the natural response to a set of accurate facts that never resolved into an actual ask — Elena had nothing specific to decide on.
items.reference:
📊 62% — a number with no reference point
❓ "Risk of exhaustion" — no date, no cost attached
🤷 Result — "keep an eye on it," no decision made

Why: the whole scenario turns on accurate facts producing zero decision — the mechanism this unit exists to fix.
items.learnMore:
Accurate but undecidable

Nothing Marcus said in the opening scenario was wrong. 62% utilization was the real number. The query-plan regression was a real, compounding factor. "Risk of connection exhaustion under peak load" was a genuine possibility. The problem is that none of those statements, individually or stacked together, told Elena what it would cost or by when she needed to decide something — so "keep an eye on it" wasn't a rejection, it was the only reasonable response available given what she'd actually been told. This is the core failure mode the rest of the unit works to fix: correctness alone doesn't produce a decision.

items.learnMore:
The two questions every ask has to answer

A business leader is constantly comparing competing claims on the same limited budget and headcount — a hiring plan, a marketing spend, another team's proposal. Every one of those arrives already denominated in cost and timeline, which is what lets the leader weigh them against each other. "62% pool utilization" isn't in that unit at all — it's a true fact about system internals that simply doesn't answer "what does this cost" or "by when." That's not a failure of clarity; a perfectly clear explanation of connection pools still wouldn't answer either question. The fix isn't clearer technical explanation, it's translation into cost and timing.

items.learnMore:
Three specific mappings, not a vague rewording

It's tempting to think "translating for business" just means using simpler words. L2's table is more specific than that: severity maps onto probability-with-a-trend, "could cause an outage" maps onto a concrete dollar-and-customer impact, and "this is urgent" maps onto an actual date. Each mapping targets a different piece of information the business leader needs, and skipping any one of the three leaves a gap — impact without a date is uncomparable to a calendar; probability without impact doesn't say what's at stake; a date without impact doesn't say why it matters.

items.learnMore:
Credibility is the resource both extremes spend

Catastrophizing and minimizing look like opposite mistakes, but they spend the same resource: the listener's trust in future warnings from the same source. The fix isn't finding a middle-ground severity word — it's reporting the actual trend, the actual projected date, and the actual cost, whatever those numbers turn out to be. Calibration isn't a compromise between the two extremes; it's refusing to round the real numbers toward either one.

The fix isn't finding a middle-ground severity word — it's reporting the actual trend, the actual projected date, and the actual cost, whatever those numbers turn out to be. Calibration isn't a compromise between the two extremes; it's refusing to round the real numbers toward either one.

It's easy to evaluate an explanation from the speaker's side — did I say something true? items.prompt: L3's extend-it question asks about reporting a newly disclosed vulnerability in a third-party library instead of a capacity risk. What does L3 say is likely different about that risk's "by when"?

items.learnMore:
One case, not the whole territory

Marcus's capacity risk is one worked example of the translation pattern, not the entire scope of what it applies to. A newly disclosed authentication-library vulnerability shares the same shape — probability, impact, a date, options — but each piece is driven by different underlying facts. Probability tracks how public and how easily exploitable the flaw is, not a traffic growth rate. Impact likely shifts from lost checkout revenue toward legal exposure and breach-notification costs if customer data is involved. The "by when" anchor changes from a projected trend line to "how fast is this becoming easier to exploit, and does a vendor patch exist yet." The reader is meant to practice re-deriving each piece for a new kind of risk, not just recall Marcus's specific numbers.
